narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the wicked man conceives evil... and gives birth to lies' - conceiving read not as a bare thought but as a gestation, harm carried and delivered. Type (102) is cognition: this is an interior mental act, evil formed in the mind before it ever shows in deed. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not trace where the conceiving springs from - no prior wound, no tempter, no drive is booked; the wicked interior is simply shown generating evil out of itself, its origin left unaccounted and the whole weight resting on the man's own generative interior. Seat (104) resolves to none: for all the womb-imagery, the operation is not lodged in a named organ - it is the whole wicked person that conceives, not a faculty switched on. Bearer (105) is 'the wicked' (inferred, to_span 283602): the interior read is the wicked man's, the one the psalm has just set opposite the righteous God who tests minds and hearts. Operation (106), the core event, is 'the wicked conceives evil, is pregnant with mischief, and gives birth to lies - harm gestated from within': a grim pregnancy, evil conceived, carried, and delivered. Target (107) is gestation-of-evil (inferred, to_span 283602): what the operation aims at is the bringing-forth itself - the object is the production of harm, evil made to term. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - not sudden, not laboured; the flat report presents the gestation as bare fact. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows the evil beyond 'mischief' and 'lies', and though the next verses show the mischief returning on his own head, the reading does not book that as this operation's effect - it holds the conceiving as generation, not yet consequence. Coupling (112) is 'conceive-and-birth' (inferred, to_span 283602): the one binding the reading registers is the weld of conception to delivery - the two are inseparable, evil conceived is evil born; there is no interior that carries evil without in the end producing it. Prohibition (113) is absent: no forbidding is attached; the verse indicts by picture, not by command. Discovery (114) names the placement: 'he conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies' - the operation a grim generation, the wicked interior gestating and delivering its harm like a pregnancy. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait of the wicked's inner being, not a passing impulse. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the whole movement sits inside, a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the wicked man's interior conceives evil, carries it as a pregnancy, and delivers it as lies - a cognitive generation welded from conception to birth, held wholly within as a settled trait of the wicked self, evil produced out of the man's own inner ground.
narratives.story: The psalm pictures the inner life of a wicked man as a kind of pregnancy. He conceives evil the way a mother conceives a child - it starts as something carried inside, in the mind, long before it is seen. Then he is pregnant with mischief, and at last he gives birth to lies. The harm is not something done to him or planted in him by anyone else; the passage never says where it comes from - it simply grows out of the man himself. It is his whole self that does this, not just one part of him. And once evil is conceived, it will be born: carrying it and delivering it are one unbroken thing. There is no measuring of how much or how fierce, and no note here of where it ends up, though the verses that follow show his mischief falling back on his own head. What the passage fixes on is the generation itself - a settled bent of the inner life that keeps producing evil from within, as naturally and inevitably as a body brings a child to term.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'Turn away from evil and do good' (ra) - evil named here not as a deed being done but as the thing the will is told to turn FROM. Type (102) is volition: unusually for this family, this is an act of the will, evil as the object of a commanded reorientation, not a settled wicked bent. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no origin for the evil - it is not traced to a drive or a tempter; it stands simply as the direction the interior is charged to abandon. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located - it is the whole self told to turn, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is 'the hearer' (inferred, to_span 277716): the interior addressed is the one who receives the charge, the reader summoned to reorient. Operation (106), the event, is 'the self is told to turn away from evil and do good, so as to dwell forever - the twofold moral turn': a double movement, away from evil and toward good. Target (107) is moral-turn (inferred, to_span 277716): what the operation aims at is the reorientation itself. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked - the command stands flatly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree scored, nothing narrows it, and 'so shall you dwell forever' is read as the charge's horizon rather than booked as this operation's effect. Coupling (112) is 'turn-and-do-good' (inferred, to_span 277716): the binding is the weld of the turn-from-evil to the doing-of-good - the two are one act, the negative and positive halves of a single reorientation; one cannot leave evil without moving toward good. Prohibition (113) is absent as a marked flag, yet the sense itself is quasi-prohibitive - 'turn away from evil.' Discovery (114): 'Turn away from evil and do good, so shall you dwell forever' - the double movement of the will, away from evil and toward good, the interior reorienting its whole direction. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing trait the inner being is charged to hold. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the turn is a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the hearer's will is commanded to turn away from evil and toward good in one welded movement - evil here read from the outside, as the thing the interior is to leave, a volitional reorientation held within as a standing posture.
narratives.story: Here evil appears from a different angle than usual - not as something a wicked person is busy doing, but as the very thing a person is told to walk away from. The command is simple and double: turn away from evil, and do good. It is an act of the will, a decision to change direction. And the two halves belong together - you cannot really leave evil behind without at the same time moving toward good; they are one turn, not two. The passage does not say where the evil came from or how hard the turning is; it just issues the charge and holds out its promise, that the one who turns will dwell secure for good. What it fixes on is the reorientation itself, a settled inward direction the person is called to take and keep.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of thirteen distinct readings of evil (ra) in the family, and it is the outlier. Where the other twelve read evil as a settled wickedness borne by the wicked or the enemies (a status or disposition of theirs), this reading alone reads evil as VOLITION - not evil possessed but evil renounced, the object of a commanded turn. The bearer is not a wicked man but 'the hearer' summoned to reorient; the direction is away from evil, not toward it. The difference is the finding: the same word names both the thing the wicked cling to and the thing the righteous will is charged to abandon.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'evils have encompassed me... my iniquities have overtaken me... my heart fails' (ra) - evil here read as an engulfing mass that overwhelms the self. Type (102) is state: not a deed and not a settled wickedness, but a condition suffered, the interior swamped. Source (103) is absent: the reading does not trace where the flood of evils originates - notably it does not separate the psalmist's own iniquities from outward troubles as their spring; both are named but their origin is left unbooked, the report holding the inundation itself rather than its cause. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located, though 'heart' is named - the failing heart reads as the whole inner person giving out, not a faculty malfunctioning. Bearer (105) is 'the psalmist' (inferred, to_span 278245): the interior read is the sufferer's own, buried under his guilt. Operation (106), the event, is 'evils have encompassed the self beyond number; its iniquities have overtaken it till it cannot see, more than the hairs of its head, so its heart fails - being swamped by guilt': inundation, the self buried. Target (107) is swamped-by-guilt (inferred, to_span 278245): what the operation lands on is the self overwhelmed. Manner (108) is none: no mode is marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent as marked flags - yet the sense itself carries an unmeasured extremity ('beyond number,' 'more than the hairs of my head,' 'my heart fails'); the reading reports that extremity in the sense-line without booking a separate degree or downstream outcome. Coupling (112) is 'iniquities-overwhelm' (inferred, to_span 278245): the binding welds the evils to the overwhelming - the guilt and the drowning are inseparable, the mass of iniquity being precisely what buries the courage. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'my iniquities have overtaken me, till I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me' - the operation is inundation, the interior buried under uncountable guilt and its courage giving out. Role (115) is characteristic: a standing condition, not a passing pang. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the psalmist's own iniquities and encompassing evils overtake him beyond counting until he cannot see and his heart fails - evil read here not as something done but as an engulfing state, guilt welded to the drowning of the self, held wholly within as the collapse of inner courage.
narratives.story: This is evil felt from the inside as being drowned. The man is not doing wrong here - he is buried under it. Troubles have surrounded him past counting, and his own sins have caught up with him until he cannot even see; there are more of them, he says, than the hairs on his head, and his heart gives out. The passage does not sort out where it all comes from or separate his own guilt from the troubles pressing in; it simply reports the flood. The sheer, unmeasured weight of it is the point - too many to number, enough to make his courage fail. And the guilt and the drowning are one thing: it is exactly the mass of his iniquity that swamps him. This is evil as an overwhelming condition of the inner life, a man going under.
narratives.variation_note: Against the family's twelve other readings of evil (ra), this one is distinctive in type and direction. It is not the wicked's settled bent nor the enemies' malice aimed outward, but a STATE the psalmist suffers - his own iniquities turned back on him as an engulfing flood. Where most readings locate evil in a hostile 'them,' here it overtakes the 'I,' and where most read it as status or disposition, here it is a condition of collapse. The difference marks how the same word can name both the evil the wicked wield and the evil that buries the penitent under his own guilt.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness' (resha) - wickedness named not as something the bearer does but as the thing the righteous king abhors. Type (102) is status: wickedness as a moral condition, an abstract evil, here appearing as an object rather than an act. Source (103) is absent: no origin for the wickedness is booked; it stands simply as the moral opposite the king rejects. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is booked oddly as 'wickedness (the king's hatred)' (inferred, to_span 278988): the reading reads the interior through the king's HATRED of wickedness - the operation of the inner being caught here is the righteous recoil, wickedness present only as its object. Operation (106) is none (resolution none): no wicked act is performed - fittingly, for in this passage wickedness is not being done but being hated; the reading marks the absence of any operation by wickedness itself. Target (107) is none: no target, again fitting - the wickedness here acts on nothing; it is acted upon, the object of hatred. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no outcome - the reading holds wickedness as a static moral object, not a moving force. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 278988 to_span 278987): it is 'the object of the king's hatred' - wickedness welded to the king's hating of it, paired with the righteousness he loves; the two are set as poles, and wickedness registers only in that opposition. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'and hated wickedness (resha)' - the evil the king abhors, resha here the object of his righteous hatred, the moral opposite his heart rejects. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: with no source, no operation, and no target of its own, wickedness appears in this reading not as a force but as an object - the thing a righteous heart hates, welded to the righteousness it loves, registered wholly through the king's inward recoil from it. The near-total silence (operation none, target none, manner none) is itself the finding: read from the righteous side, wickedness does nothing; it is simply hated.
narratives.story: This is wickedness seen from the opposite side - not as something a bad man is doing, but as the thing a good king cannot stand. The line says he has loved righteousness and hated wickedness, and that hatred is the real subject here. Wickedness itself does nothing in this scene: it has no plan, no victim, no force of its own. It shows up only as the object the king's heart rejects, the exact opposite of the goodness he loves. The two are set against each other like poles, and what the passage actually shows us is the inner recoil of a righteous person - the settled turning-away that is the flip side of loving what is right. Wickedness is present only as the thing being refused.
narratives.variation_note: This item has two distinct readings. Here at Psa 45:7 wickedness (resha) is read from the RIGHTEOUS side - it does nothing (operation none, target none), appearing only as the object of the good king's hatred, welded to the righteousness he loves. At Psa 125:3 (reading #2) the same word is read from the active side, as the 'scepter of wickedness,' an oppressive dominion that rules over the righteous' land until God limits it. The difference is stark: in one the interior caught is a righteous heart recoiling from wickedness; in the other it is wickedness itself enthroned and pressing down. One word, seen once as hated object and once as ruling force.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'But to the wicked God says: What right have you to recite my statutes?' (rasha) - the wicked here the religious hypocrite who mouths the covenant while living in sin. Type (102) is status: a standing moral condition of the person, not a single act. Source (103) is absent: no origin for the wickedness is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located - it is the person as such, not an inner organ. Bearer (105) is 'the wicked' (inferred, to_span 279525): the interior read is the hypocrite's. Operation (106) is none (resolution none): the reading marks that no wicked deed is the focus here - the indictment falls on the wicked's STATUS as one who has no right to recite God's statutes, not on a particular act; the emptiness is telling, the man condemned for what he is while performing religion. Target (107) is none: no target booked - his wickedness is not aimed outward in this verse but exposed as his own condition. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no outcome. Coupling (112) is none (resolution none): the reading books no companion condition here - the wicked stands exposed alone, his religion and his life set against each other by the following verses but not welded in this row. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'But to the wicked (rasha) God says: What right have you to recite my statutes?' - the hypocrite who mouths God's covenant while living in sin, rasha here the one whose reciting of the law is condemned by his conduct - religion without obedience. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:person - notably, the wicked here is placed OUTSIDE, as another person over against the psalm's God-addressing voice, not an interior state read from within. The full process: with no source, no operation, no target, and no coupling booked, the reading holds the wicked almost purely as a status - a person whose whole condition is condemned, the hypocrite who recites God's statutes while hating discipline; the near-silence across the dimensions fixes the finding on WHAT he is rather than what he does, and locates him as an external figure exposed by God's own address.
narratives.story: God turns and speaks directly to a certain kind of person: the wicked one who keeps reciting God's laws and taking his covenant on his lips - and God asks what right he has to do it. The passage does not point to one particular crime here. It condemns the man for what he is: someone who performs religion while his life runs the other way, who hates correction and throws God's words behind him even as he mouths them. He is not caught doing a single deed; he is exposed as a whole - a hypocrite, religion without obedience. And he stands here as an outsider, another person God addresses across the room, not an inner life described from within. The silence about any specific act is the point: it is his condition, not his conduct in this moment, that is on trial.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'the wicked' (rasha) in the family. This reading is distinctive for what it does NOT book - operation none, target none, coupling none - holding the wicked almost purely as a STATUS, and for its locus external:person, placing him as a figure God addresses rather than an interior read from within. Where other readings catch the wicked in an act (oppressing, exulting, forsaking the law, perishing), here the whole indictment falls on the hypocrite's condition: a man who recites the covenant while living in sin. The near-total dimensional silence is itself the finding - the wicked condemned for what he is, not for a deed.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'You give your mouth free rein for evil' (ra) - evil here the unbridled wicked speech the mouth pours out. Type (102) is status: a settled condition of the wicked, here shown issuing through the tongue. Source (103) is absent: no origin booked for the evil. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located - though the mouth and tongue are named, they are instruments, not a seat where the operation is lodged. Bearer (105) is 'the wicked (his mouth)' (inferred, to_span 279549): the interior read is the wicked's, expressed through his speech. Operation (106) is 'give free rein to' (inferred, to_span 279549): the event is the loosing - the mouth set unbridled to evil, no restraint on the tongue. Target (107) is none: no single target booked in this row, though the next verse names brother and kin - the loosing is read as the act itself, its object left to the pairing. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no outcome. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 279549 to_span 279552): it is 'paired with the tongue framing deceit' - the evil-loosed mouth is welded to the deceit-framing tongue; the two work together, unbridled evil speech and calculated lying inseparable. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'You give your mouth free rein for evil (ra)' - unbridled wicked speech, ra here the evil the mouth pours out, the tongue set loose for harm, framing deceit against brother and kin. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the evil is a condition of the inner life, issuing outward through speech. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the wicked looses his mouth to evil, welding that unbridled speech to a tongue that frames deceit - evil here read as speech uncurbed, a settled inward condition that pours out through the mouth against brother and kin.
narratives.story: This is evil that comes out of the mouth. God charges the wicked man with giving his mouth free rein - letting his speech run loose with no brake on it - and with a tongue that frames deceit. The two go together: the unbridled talk and the careful lying are one operation, and in the next breath the passage shows where it lands, against his own brother and his mother's son. The evil is not traced to any cause here; it is simply a settled condition of the man that spills out in words. What the passage catches is the loosing itself - a mouth let off the leash for harm, an inner corruption that shows itself in what he says.
narratives.variation_note: Among the thirteen evil (ra) readings, this one fixes on evil as SPEECH - the mouth given free rein, welded to the deceit-framing tongue. Where #1 is evil renounced by the will and #2 is evil as a flood that buries the psalmist, here evil is the wicked's own unbridled utterance aimed at brother and kin. The distinctive coupling (evil-loosed mouth bound to the lying tongue) marks how this reading operates: evil not merely held but poured out in words.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'and done what is evil in your sight' (ra) - evil here the deed judged wrong by God's own eyes, owned by the penitent about himself. Type (102) is status: the moral quality of what he has done, a wrongness measured before God. Source (103) is absent: no origin for the evil is booked - the psalm elsewhere reaches back to being 'brought forth in iniquity,' but this row does not trace the deed to that source; it holds the confession, not its genealogy. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is 'the penitent' (inferred, to_span 279740): strikingly, the bearer of the evil here is the psalmist himself - this is the family's evil owned in the first person, not projected onto enemies. Operation (106) is 'done' (inferred, to_span 279740): the event is the committing - evil enacted, now confessed. Target (107) is 'in God's sight' (inferred, to_span 279740): what the evil is oriented to is God's own judgment - the deed done before his eyes, measured by his standard. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no separate outcome - the reading holds the confession itself. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 279740 to_span 279738): it is 'paired with against you only have I sinned' - the evil-done welded to the confession that the sin is ultimately against God alone; the deed and its Godward direction are inseparable. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'and done what is evil (ra) in your sight' - the deed judged evil by God's own eyes, ra here the wrong measured not by human opinion but before God, the standard against which the penitent condemns himself. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the evil's reference-point sits OUTSIDE the self, in God's judgment; its wrongness is fixed by his sight, not the self's estimate. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the penitent owns that he has DONE evil - not the enemies' evil but his own - and locates its wrongness wholly in God's sight, welding the deed to the confession that his sin is against God alone; evil here read in the first person, its measure and reference external, lodged in the eyes of the God he has wronged.
narratives.story: This is the rare place where evil is not somebody else's - it is the speaker's own, confessed. He says plainly that he has done what is evil in God's sight. What makes it evil is not what people think of it, but that God saw it: the deed is measured against God's own eyes. And he binds this admission to another - that his sin is, in the end, against God alone. The two belong together: the wrong he did and the fact that it was done before God are one thing. He does not here explain how he came to it; he simply owns it. This is evil turned inward and upward at once - a man judging himself by God's standard and naming his own act for what it is.
narratives.variation_note: This reading is distinctive among the thirteen evil (ra) readings for its BEARER and its locus. Alone with #1 and #2 it turns the word away from the enemies: here the penitent owns the evil as his own DEED, done 'in God's sight,' and the locus is external:god - the evil's measure fixed in God's judgment rather than in an inner state. Where most readings read evil as the wicked's settled malice, this reads it as confessed guilt, the first-person admission that welds the deed to 'against you only have I sinned.' The variation shows the same word serving both accusation of enemies and self-accusation before God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man?' (ra) - evil here the wickedness that is the object of the tyrant's pride. Type (102) is status: a settled condition, the evil the tyrant glories in. Source (103) is absent: no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is 'the tyrant' (inferred, to_span 279799): the interior read is the mighty man's, the Doeg of the heading who gloried in his malice. Operation (106) is 'boasted in' (inferred, to_span 279799): the event is the boasting - evil not hidden but paraded, made the ground of pride. Target (107) is none: no outward victim booked in this row - the boasting turns evil into a badge, the object being the evil itself rather than a person struck. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no outcome. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 279799 to_span 279813): it is 'the evil he boasts in, and later loves (v3)' - the boasted-in evil welded to the evil he is said to LOVE in v3; boasting and love of evil are bound as one settled bent. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'boast in evil (ra), O mighty man' - the wickedness that is the object of his pride, ra here the mischief the tyrant glories in, the same evil he is later said to love more than good (v3), the settled bent of his heart. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the evil is a condition of the inner life, here surfacing as pride. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the tyrant BOASTS in evil, making his wickedness the ground of his pride and welding that boast to the love of evil confessed in v3 - evil here read as the object of glory, a settled inward bent that the mighty man parades rather than hides.
narratives.story: This is evil worn as a boast. The psalm confronts a powerful man who is proud of his own wickedness - he brags about it. Evil, for him, is not something to hide but something to show off, a badge of his strength. The passage ties this boasting to what it says a moment later: that he actually loves evil more than good. The two belong together - to boast in evil and to love it are one settled bent of his heart. There is no victim named in this particular line and no explaining where it came from; the point is simply that his wickedness has become his pride. This is the inner life of a man so far gone that his evil is his glory.
narratives.variation_note: This reading and its neighbour #6 (Psa 52:3) catch the same tyrant in one psalm and are deliberately welded to each other (the boasted-in evil of v1 paired with the loved evil of v3). Among the thirteen evil (ra) readings this pair is distinctive for reading evil as the object of PRIDE and LOVE - not evil done to a victim but evil embraced as glory and preference. #5 fixes on the boasting, #6 on the loving; the difference between them is the finding, showing evil's hold on the interior as both paraded pride (v1) and settled affection (v3).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'You love evil more than good' (ra) - evil here the object of the tyrant's love, preferred over good. Type (102) is status: a settled condition, evil as what the heart prefers. Source (103) is absent: no origin booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located - it is the man's love, not a faculty-organ. Bearer (105) is 'the tyrant' (inferred, to_span 279813): the same mighty man of v1, his interior read again. Operation (106) is 'loved' (inferred, to_span 279813): the event is the loving - evil made the object of affection, chosen over good. Target (107) is none: no outward victim booked - the love rests on evil itself. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent as marked flags, though 'more than good' carries a comparative weight the reading holds in the sense-line rather than booking as a scored degree. Coupling (112) carries a value and is a span-resolved pair (from_span 279813 to_span 279799): it is 'the evil boasted in (v1), now loved' - the loved evil welded back to the boasted evil of v1; boasting and love are the two faces of one bent. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): 'You love evil (ra) more than good' - the evil that is the object of his love, ra here what the tyrant prefers over good, the same mischief he boasted in (v1), now shown as the settled preference of his heart. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the tyrant LOVES evil more than good, his affection settled on wickedness itself - the same evil he boasted in now shown as his heart's preference; evil here read as the object of a disordered love, an inward bent welded to the pride of v1.
narratives.story: A step deeper than the boast: this man does not merely brag about evil, he loves it - and loves it more than good. His affection is set on wickedness itself; given the choice between good and evil, his heart leans to evil. The passage ties this back to his boasting a moment earlier: the pride and the love are two sides of one settled bent. Nothing here explains how his heart got this way, and no single victim is in view; the point is the preference itself. This is the inner life of a man whose deepest liking has been turned upside down, so that the wrong thing is the thing he most wants.
narratives.variation_note: The twin of #5 within Psa 52, explicitly welded to it: #5 reads the tyrant's BOASTING in evil (v1), this reads his LOVING evil more than good (v3). The distinction is the finding - boasting parades evil outward as glory, love fixes it inward as preference. Together they show, against the family's other evil (ra) readings, evil not as a deed aimed at a victim but as the object of a corrupted heart's pride and desire.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'They are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity' (taab) - abominable naming the loathsome, God-detestable quality of the fools' deeds. Type (102) is action: this is a doing, deeds practised, not a mere state. Source (103) is absent: no origin booked for the abominable-doing, though the verse traces it to the heart that says 'there is no God' - the reading holds the deed, not its root. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is 'the fools' (inferred, to_span 279887): the interior read is the God-denying fools'. Operation (106) is 'do / practise' (event): the deeds are enacted, abomination made habitual. The loathsome deeds and the inner corruption belong together; the vile behaviour is simply the outward face of a heart that has decided God is not there. Strip away the belief in God, the passage says, and this is what comes out - conduct God finds detestable.

These are godless men bearing down on the psalmist - their clamour and the trouble they keep dropping on him are one thing, a steady hostile pressure. It is aimed straight at him. Here the wicked are simply the ones leaning their whole hostility onto a man until he is overwhelmed.

The most telling thing is what is not said - evil here is not doing anything; it is simply dwelling in them.

So the evil is both the direction of their thoughts and the thing that makes them guilty. What is caught here is a mind wholly given over to plotting harm against another person.

What is caught here is not a deed but a reckoning, the guilt of the wicked hanging over them and sure to be called in.

narratives.story: This psalm looks at wicked people and traces their corruption all the way back to birth. They are, it says, estranged from the womb - they go astray from the day they are born, speaking lies as soon as they can. The point is that their wickedness is not something they picked up along the way; it is built in, present from the start. The passage does not describe one particular crime here - it describes a nature, a settled condition that shows itself early in straying and lying. And it looks ahead to how such wickedness is stopped: not by reform but by God breaking their fangs, the way you would draw the teeth of a venomous snake. This is the wicked read at their root, corrupt from the beginning.

Evil here is their occupation - iniquity is what they do, their trade. And the passage sets it next to bloodthirst: the working of wickedness and the appetite for killing are one company, inseparable. He does not spell out how they came to this; he simply names them as workers of iniquity and murderous men, and asks God to save him from them. What is caught is a settled condition of the inner life that expresses itself as a livelihood of harm, sharpened here by the thirst for blood.

The people, feeling that God has rejected them and no longer marches with their armies, come to a hard, honest conclusion: human rescue is worthless. Whatever help men can give is, they say, vanity. It is a judgment they reach in their own minds, a disillusioned but true estimate. And it is set as the exact opposite of the next line, where with God they will do valiantly. The collapse of human hope and the turn to God are two sides of one coin. What is caught here is the moment a community stops trusting in human deliverance and, by stripping that false hope away, clears the ground for confidence in God alone.

What is caught here is the wicked at their end - not doing anything, but coming undone before a God whose nearness they cannot survive.

What is caught is the wicked as a looming threat from outside - a hostile presence pressing on a vulnerable man who has nowhere to turn but God.

They have no pain, their bodies are healthy and sleek, they are not in trouble like everyone else. Their ease is the thing that caught him - it seemed to make faith pointless. And that prosperity does not sit quietly; it breeds arrogance. Pride becomes their necklace, violence their clothing, and they scoff and threaten. The comfort and the contempt go together. What is caught here is the wicked not in a particular crime but in their untroubled flourishing - the scandal of the godless doing well, which nearly overturned the psalmist's faith until he went into God's presence and saw their end.

The warning is bound to what comes later: it is God who lifts one up and puts another down, and in the end he will cut off the horns of the wicked. So the arrogant strength they are warned about is the very thing the Judge will one day break. What is caught here is the wicked at the moment of warning - their proud self-assertion named and forbidden by the God who has the power to humble them.

What is caught is the inner reality of the guilty who benefit from corruption - the wicked man whose escape from justice is itself the wrong being exposed.

narratives.story: This is one of the darkest of the psalms, and it opens with a man saying his soul is full of troubles and his life is nearly at the grave. The word here is the same one used elsewhere for evil, but there is no wrongdoing in view - only suffering. His inner self is crowded, filled to the brim with troubles, so packed with them that death feels close. The passage does not say where they came from; it just reports the fullness. And the troubles and the soul that holds them cannot be separated - his very condition is a self overrun with them. What is caught here is not wickedness done but evil endured, a person weighed down with trouble until he stands at the edge of the pit.

It is not that he has done something loathsome - it is that his affliction has turned him into an object others recoil from. And it comes bound to another misery: he is shut in, unable to escape. The revulsion of his friends and his own trapped isolation go together. What is caught here is abandonment at its sharpest - a man so afflicted that those who loved him now turn away, and he is left detestable and alone.

The quick growth is not a sign of strength but of shallowness - grass that shoots up and is gone. Their flourishing and their ruin are the same story. What looks like the wicked doing well is really the wicked hastening their own end. The passage sets their bloom next to the brief flourishing of all evildoers, and reads both the same way: a fast, showy rise that runs straight to being cut down forever.

What is caught is the wicked as the object of a righteous ruler's determination to purge them, so that no evil is allowed to settle in God's place.

What is caught is the wicked as slanderers, their hostility taking the form of words - and against it the psalmist sets not counter-attack but prayer, giving himself to God while their mouths keep accusing.

narratives.story: As the psalm prays for its enemies to be repaid, it names them once more: those who speak evil against my life. Evil here is malice carried in speech, and it is aimed at the highest stake - his life itself. Their words are not idle insults but an assault meant to destroy him. The evil and the accusers who utter it are named as one; the malice belongs to them. This is the ground on which the psalmist asks God to make all their curses recoil - let this evil speech be the very reward the LORD hands back to them. What is caught is the accusers' settled hostility expressed in words that seek a man's undoing.
narratives.variation_note: The last of the thirteen evil (ra) readings, and one of three in Psa 109. Like #12 it reads evil as DISPOSITION carried by the accusers, but where #12 fixes on the perverse exchange (evil for good), this fixes on evil SPEECH aimed 'against my life.' The variation across Psa 109 shows the enemies' evil named successively as ingratitude (#12) and as life-threatening accusation (#13) - the same disposition caught at different points of its assault.

narratives.story: The whole psalm has praised the blessed, righteous man - secure, generous, unafraid - and it ends by turning to his opposite: the wicked man sees all this and is enraged. He watches the good man's blessing, and instead of being drawn to it he is galled by it; he gnashes his teeth and melts away. His anger is the anger of one who cannot bear another's good and has no share in it. And that very rage is bound up with his undoing - he melts, and his desire comes to nothing. What is caught here is the wicked as the envious foil to the blessed, consumed from within by fury at a goodness he will never possess.

narratives.story: Across this long psalm the wicked keep reappearing as the antagonist of the man who loves God's law, and this line gathers them up: hot indignation seizes him because of the wicked, who forsake God's law. Two things go together in them - they abandon the law themselves, and they lay traps for him. Their defection from God and their hostility to the psalmist are one and the same movement. And they recur throughout the psalm: their cords try to ensnare him, they lie in ambush to destroy him, they set snares in his path, yet he does not forget or stray from the law. What is caught is the wicked as the standing foe of the faithful - law-forsakers whose abandonment of God burns the psalmist with indignation while their snares fail to move him.
narratives.variation_note: This single reading is the anchor for the whole wicked-foe arc of Psalm 119, recurring at 119:61 (their cords ensnare), 119:95 (they lie in ambush to destroy), 119:110 (they lay a snare), 119:119 (the wicked discarded like dross), and 119:155 (salvation far from the wicked). Rather than several distinct readings, the psalm treats the wicked as one consistent antagonist across its length, so the recurrences share this anchor's reading. Among the seventeen rasha readings it is distinctive for coupling to a whole recurring arc rather than a single scene, and for provoking the psalmist's 'hot indignation' as the interior response to law-forsaking.

narratives.story: In a psalm full of the wicked and their snares, this line gives the answer from the other side: I hold back my feet from every evil way, in order to keep your word. Here the movement is not toward evil but away from it, and it is deliberate - the psalmist actively restrains himself, pulling his feet back from every path that would lead him wrong. And the reason is love for God's word: he refuses evil precisely so that he can keep it. This restraint is part of the whole shape of his devotion across the psalm. Against all the wickedness the psalm describes, this is the inner being's counter-move - a man curbing himself from evil for the sake of obeying God.

narratives.story: The psalmist, devoted to God's law, draws a line against a certain company: depart from me, you evildoers, that I may keep the commandments of my God. The evildoers are named by what they do - evil is their settled practice - and it presses on him closely enough that he must send them away. He treats their company as a threat to his obedience: to keep God's commands, he has to be rid of them. So he pushes them outside, out of his life. What is caught here is evil-doing as the mark of a company the faithful must separate from - not analysed from within, but held at arm's length, banished so that a man can hold on to his God.

narratives.story: This song of ascents pictures wickedness as a ruler's scepter stretched over the land given to God's people. It is oppressive power - wickedness in the seat of authority, pressing down on the righteous. But the promise is that it will not rest there for good: God will not let the rule of the wicked settle permanently over his people's land. And the reason given is tender and shrewd - lest the righteous themselves, worn down under long oppression, be tempted to reach out their own hands to do wrong. So God caps the tenure of wicked rule not only to spare his people harm but to guard their integrity. What is caught is wickedness as dominion, and the mercy of the limit God sets on it.
narratives.variation_note: The second of the two wickedness (resha) readings, and the active counterpart to #1 (Psa 45:7). Where #1 read wickedness from the righteous side - a static object hated by the good king, doing nothing - here it is read from the active side, an oppressive 'scepter' ruling over the righteous' land. The difference is stark: hated object versus ruling force. This reading also carries the distinctive note of the LIMIT God sets on wicked rule, for the sake of the righteous' integrity - wickedness enthroned but capped.

narratives.story: The psalm ends by sorting people according to their ways. God does good to those who are good and upright in heart; but those who turn aside to crooked paths, he will lead away with the evildoers. The evildoers here are the settled workers of iniquity, and the point is that the turncoats - people who bend from the straight way - end up removed right along with them, sharing one fate. What is caught is the evildoers at the moment of judgment's sorting: God leads them off, and any who have turned crooked go with them, so that peace can rest on his people. The workers of iniquity are read here not in an act of harm but in their removal, gathered up and led away.

narratives.story: Israel remembers a long history of affliction - greatly have they oppressed me from my youth, plowers plowing long furrows on my back - and then names the deliverance: the LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked. Here the wicked are seen through their instrument, the cords with which they held the people bound, their oppression pictured as ropes. And the turning point is God's act: being righteous, he cuts those cords and undoes the binding. The wicked's grip and its severing are the whole story. What is caught is the wicked as oppressors whose hold on God's people is real but not final - ropes that a righteous God simply cuts through, setting the bound free.
narratives.variation_note: A rasha reading that catches the wicked through their INSTRUMENT of oppression - the 'cords' that bind Israel - and through their undoing, the righteous LORD cutting those cords. It differs from the doom-readings that dissolve the wicked (#4, #10) by fixing on the breaking of their grip rather than their destruction, and from the oppressor-readings (#2, #9) by imaging the oppression as binding ropes severed by God. The finding is the wicked's hold shown real but not final.

narratives.story: Psalm 139 has spent itself in wonder - God knowing the psalmist completely, forming him in the womb, thoughts toward him past counting - and then it turns sharply: O that you would slay the wicked, O God; depart from me, you men of blood. The wicked here are the bloodthirsty, and what the psalmist recoils from is not one crime but their whole bent - a settled inner orientation toward killing that defines them as men of blood. Their disposition and their thirst for blood are one thing. Having just contemplated the God who gives and knows life, he cannot abide those whose inmost bearing is set toward taking it. What is caught is the wicked read at the level of disposition, a murderous heart the psalmist wants nothing to do with.
narratives.variation_note: Uniquely among the seventeen rasha readings, this one is typed as DISPOSITION - the wicked read not as a status nor caught in an act but as bearers of a settled 'murderous bent,' welded to bloodthirst. Where most readings fix on what the wicked do or suffer, this fixes on their inner orientation itself. Its placement is also distinctive: it erupts from a psalm of wonder at God's knitting of life, the recoil from men of blood set against the marvel of being made - the disposition toward killing rejected by one who has just contemplated the giving of life.
